issues.title: Hardcoded Secrets in .env.local Tracked in Git
issues.message: The .env.local file containing NEXTAUTH_SECRET and Google OAuth credentials is present in the repository and may be tracked. Additionally, NEXTAUTH_SECRET is exposed in DEPLOYMENT.md documentation.
issues.suggestion:
1. Immediately rotate NEXTAUTH_SECRET and Google OAuth credentials
2. Ensure .env.local is gitignored (currently appears to be)
3. Remove NEXTAUTH_SECRET from DEPLOYMENT.md
4. Use placeholder values in documentation
5. Store production secrets in Vercel environment variables only
6. Verify .env.local is not in git history: git log --all --full-history -- .env.local

issues.title: Missing CSRF Protection in NextAuth Configuration
issues.message: NextAuth.js is configured without explicit CSRF token validation. While NextAuth v5 beta has built-in CSRF protection, it's not explicitly configured or verified in the codebase.
issues.suggestion:
1. Verify NextAuth v5 beta CSRF protection is active
2. Add explicit useSecureCookies: true in production
3. Consider adding custom CSRF middleware for API routes
4. Test CSRF protection with security scanner

issues.title: OAuth State Parameter Not Explicitly Validated
issues.message: The OAuth flow uses 'prompt: consent' and 'response_type: code' but doesn't show explicit state parameter validation to prevent CSRF attacks during OAuth callback.
issues.suggestion:
1. Verify NextAuth handles state parameter internally (it should in v5)
2. Add unit tests to verify state validation
3. Consider adding custom state validation in jwt callback
4. Document OAuth security controls

issues.title: Session Cookie Security - SameSite 'lax' in Production
issues.message: Session cookie is configured with sameSite: 'lax' which provides less protection against CSRF than 'strict'. While 'lax' is appropriate for OAuth flows, it should be documented.
issues.suggestion:
1. Document why 'lax' is chosen (OAuth redirects)
2. Consider 'strict' if OAuth flow allows
3. Ensure secure flag is always true in production
4. Add cookie security tests

issues.title: Console.error Used for Authentication Errors
issues.message: Authentication errors are logged to console.error in multiple components (LoginForm.tsx:51, sign-out-button.tsx:80, sign-in-button.tsx:75) which could expose sensitive error details in production.
issues.suggestion:
1. Replace console.error with proper logging service
2. Sanitize error messages before logging
3. Use different log levels for development vs production
4. Implement structured logging for auth events
5. Never log tokens, session IDs, or credentials

issues.title: User Data Display Without Explicit XSS Protection
issues.message: User name, email, and image URL from Google OAuth are displayed in components without explicit sanitization. While React escapes by default, there's no validation that Google data is safe.
issues.suggestion:
1. Add input validation in User entity for name length and characters
2. Validate image URLs before rendering (check domain whitelist)
3. Add CSP headers to prevent XSS if injected
4. Sanitize user.getDisplayName() output with DOMPurify if ever used in rich text
5. Document reliance on React's automatic escaping

issues.title: Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints
issues.message: No rate limiting is visible on /api/auth endpoints which could allow brute force attacks on OAuth flows or session enumeration.
issues.suggestion:
1. Add rate limiting middleware for /api/auth routes
2. Implement exponential backoff for failed attempts
3. Use Vercel Edge Config or Upstash Rate Limit
4. Monitor and alert on suspicious auth patterns
5. Consider adding CAPTCHA after repeated failures

issues.title: JWT Access Token Stored in Session Without Encryption
issues.message: Google OAuth access token is stored in JWT token (line 33 in auth.ts) and potentially exposed to client-side code. While JWT is signed, the token is base64-encoded (not encrypted).
issues.suggestion:
1. Avoid storing access_token in JWT if not needed
2. If required, encrypt access_token before storing
3. Use server-side only session strategy for sensitive tokens
4. Implement token rotation
5. Document why access_token is needed in session

positiveFindings.title: Strong Domain Layer Validation
positiveFindings.description: User and Session entities have comprehensive validation including email format, name length, and session expiry checks. This prevents invalid data from entering the system.

positiveFindings.title: Secure Cookie Configuration
positiveFindings.description: Session cookies are configured with httpOnly: true, preventing client-side JavaScript access and mitigating XSS session theft.

positiveFindings.title: Middleware-Based Route Protection
positiveFindings.description: middleware.ts properly protects routes with session checks and redirects unauthenticated users to login with callback URL.

positiveFindings.title: OAuth Best Practices
positiveFindings.description: OAuth flow uses authorization code flow (response_type: 'code') instead of implicit flow, which is more secure.

positiveFindings.title: No dangerouslySetInnerHTML on User Data
positiveFindings.description: The single use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML is for static theme initialization code, not user-generated content.

positiveFindings.title: .env Files Properly Gitignored
positiveFindings.description: The .gitignore includes .env*.local and .env patterns, preventing accidental commit of environment files.

agentic_security_notes.reason: This is a standard web application without AI agents, LLM integrations, or MCP servers. OWASP Agentic Security Top 10 (2026) does not apply.

immediate: Rotate NEXTAUTH_SECRET and Google OAuth credentials immediately
Remove secrets from DEPLOYMENT.md and replace with placeholders
Verify .env.local is not in git history
short_term: Add structured logging service to replace console.error
Add CSP headers to prevent XSS
Write security tests for OAuth flow (state, CSRF, token validation)
long_term: Implement token encryption for OAuth access tokens
Regular dependency audits with npm audit or Snyk

rating_explanation: The Google OAuth implementation follows most security best practices with good domain validation, secure cookies, and route protection. However, CRITICAL issues exist: secrets are exposed in repository files (.env.local, DEPLOYMENT.md) which must be rotated immediately. Once secrets are rotated and removed from documentation, this would be a PASS. The remaining issues (rate limiting, logging, token encryption) are important but not blockers.
